12728-the-high-school-boys-canoe-club:
Dick and Co. take to Lake Pleasant in this Gridley tale of canoes, races, and rivals. A grand war canoe, bought with high hopes, capsizes when the boys turn together to greet the schoolgirls, and the loss stings. Schemes, bonfires, and a Trentville trip keep the club busy.

Ripley, the rich rival, tries coaxing and lies to spoil their fun, while Susie and Laura add wit to the lakeside scenes. Hancock balances sport, pranks, and fair play as the boys rebuild their standing. The story reads as a sunny summer adventure with a firm moral about pluck after a spill.
12952-four-boy-hunters-or-the-outing-of-:
Captain Ralph Bonehill's Four Boy Hunters, first volume of the Boy Hunters series, sends Snap, Shep, Whopper, and Giant out with the gun club. Target shooting, a sawmill fire, a lost boat, a first night in camp, a strange animal, and a wildcat fill the chapters. A cave, a deer hunt, rival campers, and a forest fire close the book. The preface promises big-game searching in field and forest.

Jed Sanborn, a bachelor hunter and trapper living two miles from Lake Cameron, greets the boys from his canoe, good shot and good humour both. A beastly night of rain sets the camp's temper. The book offers sturdy outdoor fun for young hunters.
14317-the-sorcery-club:
Elliott O'Donnell's 1912 novel The Sorcery Club follows seekers after Atlantis and its black art. Contents run from first hearing of Atlantis through learning to sin, tests, initiation, and first power. San Francisco ladies and divination, two dreams, love at first sight, and Leon Hamar calling on the Martians follow. O'Donnell, author of ghost books and werewolf lore, writes occult adventure with conviction.

Dreams and vanishing tricks carry the plot. Miss Rosenberg dreams a doggerel poem of a radiant maiden in a green valley, flowers her friends, brook music her lullaby, until an evil day on lonely moors. Hamar later vanishes from a railway carriage, leaving a lady to report a gentleman melted like butter in hot weather, while guards laugh and the train departs. Repeating his words backwards, Hamar reappears to greater shock. Sin, power, and love tempt the club, and Atlantis promises more than any member can safely hold.
15002-all-aboard-or-life-on-the-lake-a-s:
Oliver Optic's All Aboard, or Life on the Lake, a sequel to The Boat Club, gratifies readers curious about Wood Lake in its second season. Though a sequel, it has no direct connection with its predecessor, and its first chapter gives a synopsis of the first season for newcomers.

A new member, All Aboard and a fraternal hug open the season. Up the river, hurrah for Tony, Commodore Frank Sedley and a race follow. Little Paul, a unanimous vote, first of May, a lighthouse, a conspiracy and Rovers come next. A camp on the island closes the season. Optic writes boat-club life as teamwork, fair play and summer freedom on the water.
15562-the-s-w-f-club:
Caroline E. Jacobs, author of Joan of Jupiter Inn and Patricia, published this girls' story in 1912, with Goldsmith in Cleveland and George W. Jacobs and Company. Ten chapters run from Pauline's flag and the Maples through Uncle Paul's answer, beginnings, Bedelia, and a personally conducted tour, to Hilary's turn, snapshots, the manor, and the end of summer.

Chapter one finds Pauline dropping a napkin she is hemming, staring soberly into a rain-swept garden, while Patience upstairs sings There's a Good Time Coming during a clearing-up scrape in the garret. Pauline decides good times must be flagged, not waited for, and reaches for her writing portfolio. Jacobs writes a summer story of girls making their own fun, with letters, flags, and friendship at its heart.
21985-john-nicholson-the-lion-of-the-pun:
John Nicholson, the Lion of the Punjaub, gets a hero's life in R. E. Cholmeley's 1908 biography, written with eight colored plates. Sir Herbert Edwardes gave Lord Canning a famous judgment in March 1857. If ever a desperate deed had to be done in India, Nicholson was the man to do it. A plain stone obelisk on the Rawal Pindi road marks him still. Cholmeley's chapters run eastward ho, through the Afghan fighting and the Second Sikh War.

Nicholson as master of Bannu, with the movable column in the Mutiny, and before Delhi fill the heart of the book. He died in the hour of victory at Delhi, as the last chapter tells. Cholmeley writes open hero worship, and the plates show Nicholson adored by his men and throttling mutiny by the throat.
24840-the-re-echo-club:
Carolyn Wells published The Re-Echo Club in New York in 1913, in her Onyx Series. The club, said to follow Boston's famous Echo Club, takes known poems and rewrites them in grander styles. Its first game is Gelett Burgess's Purple Cow quatrain, redone in the voices of Milton, Shelley, and other great poets.

Later the members weigh Peter, Peter, Pumpkin Eater as a historic narrative, praising Peter's strength of character and quick decisions. Wells writes the parodies with wit and a light touch, and the club's debates are half the fun. Readers who like literary jokes will enjoy seeing small verses dressed in high poetic robes.
25577-all-adrift-or-the-goldwing-club:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, opens his Boat-Builder Series with All Adrift, or the Goldwing Club, published in Boston by Lee and Shepard. Five companion volumes follow, covering snug harbour, building a house, building a boat, rigging, and sailing.

A picture shows Pearl demanding what a boy is doing up aloft, a hint of the lively boat-club scrapes inside. Optic, known for Young America Abroad and his army, navy, and starry-flag series, writes for boys who love boats, clubs, and practical work, mixing adventure with lessons in craft and conduct.
25798-boy-scouts-in-the-north-sea-or-the:
G. Harvey Ralphson writes Boy Scouts in the North Sea, or The Mystery of a Sub, published by Donohue in Chicago and New York in 1915. Young divers attaching chains to sunken U-13 front the book.

Chapters open with a package vanishing, difficulties and dangers, and the man with the scar. The Lena Knobloch, two mysterious changes, and a difficult departure follow, with a warning from the sea and more about U-13. A strange visit and shipwreck carry boy scouts into wartime naval mystery, diving, and detection. A chapter titled Shipwreck marks a turning point late in the tale.
28554-beyond-lies-the-wub:
Philip K. Dick's short story Beyond Lies the Wub opens on a Martian loading dock, where Captain Franco's crew takes animals and birds aboard a spaceship bound for Earth. Peterson leads one last creature up the gangplank by a string: a huge, sagging, pig-like beast the natives call a wub, bought for fifty cents.

Franco calls it a dirty pig, weighing some four hundred pounds, and wonders if it is good to eat. Then the wub speaks, and the crew must reckon with a creature that talks like a philosopher. Dick's early story turns a dinner plan into a strange, funny, and unsettling debate about eating a thinking being.
31419-wyn-s-camping-days-or-the-outing-o:
Amy Bell Marlowe's Wyn's Camping Days, or The Outing of the Go-Ahead Club, published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York, is a girls' camping story. Marlowe's other books for girls include The Oldest of Four, The Girls of Hillcrest Farm, A Little Miss Nobody, and The Girl from Sunset Ranch. A frontispiece caption notes that, because the girls were in a hurry, everything seemed to go wrong, a hint of the comic mishaps ahead.

Wyn and her clubmates take to camp life with enthusiasm and a talent for trouble. Tents, cooking, hikes, and club loyalty fill the outing, while small disasters test their resourcefulness. Written for girls, the book offers wholesome adventure in the series tradition. Its charm lies in friendship under canvas, where plans go awry and the club pulls together.
32274-the-history-and-records-of-the-ele:
The History and Records of the Elephant Club was published in New York by Livermore and Rudd in 1857, with illustrations by John McLenan. It claims to be compiled from authentic documents now in the possession of the Zoological Society. Its compilers sign as Knight Russ Ockside, M.D., and Q. K. Philander Doesticks, P.B. Their names signal the book's humorous intent. The club's history is presented as a sober record, drawn from documents in a society's keeping.

Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century American humour book, a mock-chronicle of a club and its members, illustrated in the period style. The joke lies in the form: authentic documents, learned compilers, and a zoological society, all in service of club-room comedy. The Elephant Club's records survive as a specimen of the era's literary humour, when a club's minutes could become a book.
32753-croquet-as-played-by-the-newport-c:
One of the members of the Newport Croquet Club sets down the club's game, published by Sheldon and Company in New York in 1865. He writes because existing manuals fail players: Captain Mayne Reid's treatise lacks system, and American manuals leave half the ambiguous cases unsolved.

The book dwells on the right of declining and the theory of double points, by which economizing privileges breeds cunning plots and counterplots. Rules settle bridge runs, rebounds, and the tolling of the stake. The author compares whist, which taxes memory, and chess, which taxes imagination, with croquet, which joins combination and foresight to fresh air, exercise, and friendship.
34421-the-escaping-club:
Evans told the tale of his own breaks from German prison camps. His book came out in New York in 1922. He gave it to his mother, whose aid made his break work. The book was writ at her ask, he says in the gift page. Capture starts the tale, and two first camps come next.

A first break, a friend's fate, and the frontier fill part one. Pay for the try, a strafe camp, and Fort 9 come after. Tunnels, short food, and riots mark the long war years. The Bojah case and the last of Fort 9 close that part. War readers get a cool, wry voice on a hard art. Each try is told in close form.
34944-brenda-her-school-and-her-club:
Helen Leah Reed wrote Brenda, Her School and Her Club, a tale for girls issued at Boston in 1900 with pictures by Jessie Willcox Smith. Brenda Barlow and her friends at Miss Crawdon's school form a club and take up good works. Her cousin Julia comes to join the school, and the girls plan a bazaar to help a poor child named Manuel. The thirty-two chapters run through football games, a cooking class, Christmas, and a picnic at Shiloh.

The tale opens with the girls guessing what Julia will be like, Brenda cool and Nora keen to know. Reed had also written Miss Theodora, and she knew the world of school girls well. The book mixes school fun with kind deeds, and it shows what well-off city girls of 1900 thought they owed to the poor at their gates.
35374-the-dreamers-a-club:
The Dreamers: A Club is a humorous fantasy by John Kendrick Bangs, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1899. Edward Penfield drew the illustrations. The subtitle calls it a more or less faithful account of the literary exercises of the club's first regular meeting. Bangs reports the proceedings.

His other books crowd the front matter: A House-Boat on the Styx and The Pursuit of the House-Boat. Ghosts I Have Met and Peeps at People keep them company. The Dreamers gather impossible members for an evening of impossible papers. Bangs specialised in this clerking of the absurd, a humorist's ledger of ghosts, dreamers, and shades. A frontispiece introduces Cronkey Gudehart, the first gloomster. The book is a clubbable joke at the expense of every literary society that ever read minutes aloud.
36123-the-comstock-club:
Goodwin's The Comstock Club was printed at Salt Lake City in 1891 by the Tribune Job Printing Company. Goodwin edited the Salt Lake Daily Tribune, and the book's motto promises neither radiant angels nor magnified monsters, but just plain, true men. It is given to the miners of the Pacific Coast, among whom it was written, and dated December 15, 1891.

Eighteen chapters mix sketch and talk: the old flush days, the club, mirages, the argonauts, the call of the birds, specimen liars, Sister Celeste, and the humor of the West. Chapter one is a praise of the pioneer, the soldier of peace who assaults the wilderness without bugles. If he falls to forest, desert, or fever, no volleys sound over him, and the world sponges his name from its slate.
3715-the-parenticide-club:
Ambrose Bierce, the sharpest wit of American letters in his day, offers four tales in which murderers calmly explain their crimes. The club of the title is a joke with teeth, since each narrator has killed a parent and then argues, with lawyer like logic, that the deed was reasonable, even kind. A trial that drags on for seven years, a dog rendered into oil, a house fire, and a hypnotist all serve the same cold joke.

The humor is black and the prose is lean, with every excuse polished until it gleams. Bierce lets his killers condemn themselves out of their own mouths, and the comedy grows out of their total lack of shame. Readers with a taste for irony will enjoy the bite, while those who want warmth should look elsewhere, since pity has no seat at this table.
40899-the-morning-glory-club:
The Morning Glory Club is a comic novel by George Kyle, published at Boston in 1907 with a coloured frontispiece. In the town of Manville, Mrs Tweedie founds a women's club, the Morning Glories, and the chapters follow its meetings, rehearsals and big show through to a wedding and a sermon.

The book opens in the Tweedie kitchen, where Mrs Tweedie is icing a huge cake and prophesying a bronze tablet. The club, she declares, will prove false her husband's angry charge that women are the cause of all the trouble in the world. Ezra, her small and ladylike husband, agrees meekly that she always accomplishes whatever she attempts, and credits her tact, of which, he says, she has enough for two. Kyle's comedy is small-town and marital: a battle of the sexes fought with cake, minutes and amateur theatricals.
41126-the-wolf-cub:
Patrick and Terence Casey wrote a novel of Spain published at Boston in January 1918, with a frontispiece by H Weston Taylor. Little Jacinto Quesada watches his father kiss him and leave on an enterprise of forlorn desperation. The boy and his weeping mother stand on a great rock at the village edge. The father hurries down the mountainside with two trained dogs.

His work is smuggling contraband across the no man's land by Gibraltar. The village, Minas de la Sierra, sits below the snow line in the Sierra Nevada. The mother leads Jacinto to the chapel to light a candle for his father. The wolf cub of the title is the boy himself, raised amid smugglers.
42687-the-seven-sleuths-club:
Carol Norton, author of The Phantom Yacht and Bobs, A Girl Detective, wrote The Seven Sleuths' Club, issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York in 1928. Its twenty-seven chapters open with the entering of the club and run through snow maidens, a bag of gold, and two conspirators. A mystery to solve and the sleuths sleuthing follow, to home, sweet home. A front line has Merry wishing they had brought snowshoes.

The tale opens at the Sunnyside seminary, Miss Demorest's school for select young ladies, on a wild January day. A musical gong sends the girls trooping out between classes, in ribboned braids, long curls, and saucy bobs. Snow gusts through the front door bring screams of pretended fear and true delight. Norton's club of schoolgirl detectives works its cases between sleigh rides and valentine parties.
45440-note-book-no-1-of-the-kickapoo-clu:
Note-Book Number One of the Kickapoo Club was printed at Bloomington, Illinois, in 1914. The club gathered local finds and site reports from central Illinois. The front plate shows a bronze tomahawk blade found at the site of Kickapoo Fort. It also shows a granite hatchet, a flint drill, and potsherds. Some pieces rest with the McLean County Historical Society.

One paper urges help to save the great Cahokia mound group. It gives the size of Monk's Mound and notes that no spade has yet cut it. Other material came from camp sites on the Sangamon river bluffs. The book is a club record of finds, places, and care for old sites in the state.
45623-the-old-maids-club:
Zangwill wrote The Old Maids' Club, a comic novel with drawings by Townsend, with rights held from eighteen ninety-two. Zangwill had won note with The Bachelor's Club, and this book turns the same joke on young women, in a club founded by Lillie Dulcimer at age seventeen. She is sharp and self aware, and she keeps a diary meant for print.

Heads of parts play on school terms, from the maths of love to the rules of love, while Lillie and her friends talk, scheme, and weigh men, wives, and wedlock with wit. Some parts roam to an inn tale and a hunt for the Pole. The book is a light satire on clubs, courtship, and young pride.
46566-the-crime-club:
Holt White wrote The Crime Club, a tale of crime and high life issued in New York in 1910 with art by Hermann Heyer. It opens on the liner Gigantic in the Bay of Biscay, where Captain Melun is caught prying into a kit bag. A cold ring of steel at his temple tells him a Colt is held inches from his head.

The bag is Sir Paul Westerham's, and the plot soon shows him buying a whole crime syndicate. Twenty five parts bring in blackmail, a girl in the park, Scotland Yard, a gaming house, and an order from the Czar. Lady Kathleen is caught, and the Prime Minister is seized and then tells his own tale. The close is a last fight and a way out.
47166-john-dough-and-the-cherub:
Frank Baum, author of The Wizard of Oz, wrote a fairy tale printed in Chicago in 1906 with pictures by John Neill. Baum gives the book to his young friend John Randolph Reilly. The great elixir opens the tale, with two flasks and a gingerbread man named John Dough. Chick, the Cherub, joins him early, a child whose sex no one can guess, as a front picture asks.

The freaks of Phreex, a lady executioner, and a palace of romance follow. A silver pig, Pittypat and the Mifkets, an island princess, and Para Bruin the rubber bear fill the road. Fairy beavers, flamingo flights, pirate island sport, and King Dough and his court close a wild invented voyage for children.
4737-a-tale-of-a-tub:
Jonathan Swift's A Tale of a Tub, with The History of Martin, appears here in the 1889 Routledge edition, edited by Henry Morley, professor of English literature at University College London. Its contents open with dedications to Lord Somers, the bookseller to the reader, an epistle dedicatory, and a preface, followed by sections that mix tale and digression in Swift's own manner.

Sections include an introduction, a digression concerning critics, a tale of a tub, and a digression in the modern kind. Later sections add a digression in praise of digressions, a digression concerning the original, and a farther digression, before a conclusion and The History of Martin. Swift satirises religion, learning, and pride through three brothers and their coats, in prose that is witty, learned, and deliberately tangled. Readers get a classic of English satire, best read slowly, with its digressions as part of the joke.
47865-on-the-construction-of-catalogues-:
Charles Jewett, librarian of the Smithsonian Institution, wrote on the construction of catalogues of libraries in a report printed at Washington in 1853. The second edition sets out his plan for publishing catalogues by means of separate stereotyped titles. A letter and a report of commissioners front the rules. Difficulties in publishing catalogues come first, then the plan for beating them.

The same titles were to serve for general and particular catalogues alike. What sets a catalogue apart from a bibliographical dictionary is drawn with care. Rules with examples tell how titles are to be copied in full, with exactness, and repeated for every edition. Jewett's scheme aimed at one shared catalogue for all American libraries, an early dream of union lists.
48301-from-snotty-to-sub:
Heinemann published this naval memoir at London in 1918, fronted by a list of war books. Its authors had written From Dartmouth to the Dardanelles, the midshipman's log edited by his mother. A snotty is a midshipman and a sub is a sub-lieutenant, and the book walks the promotion. It is dedicated to Freddie, from his mother.

The narrator passed his medical survey in August 1915 and joined a super-dreadnought of the Grand Fleet on September the first. He had hoped for a torpedo-boat destroyer, having tasted that freer life in the Dardanelles after his last ship was sunk. The contents run from a picnic and a tragedy to a hospital ship and sick leave. Fog, naval theatricals, and the battle of Jutland fill the middle. Submarines and examinations follow, and the book ends with first experiences as a sub, the war seen from the ladder's lower rungs.
48756-by-blow-and-kiss-the-love-story-of:
By Blow and Kiss is a love tale of a man with a bad name by Boyd Cable. It ran first in parts with the name Unstable as Water in its day. A Hodder house of London and New York printed it in nineteen fourteen. Verse at its head swears the prize won by blood and sweat lies close. Heat in a tin roof hut opens the tale at a ranch meal.

Men who rode all day eat huge at a long deal board in that hut. Blazes the cook keeps their plates heap full through the meal. Scottie Mackellar, slow of word, comes last from the rail post with news. His one word on the land state is dry, and dry it long has been. A tongue tied camp waits on his slow word in the scene.
52042-reasons-why-a-churchman-may-with-g:
Reasons Why a Churchman May with Great Justice Refuse to Subscribe to the British and Foreign Bible Society is a tract printed at Yarmouth in 1817. Its writer, a minister of a populous parish, says he was pressed to make his reasons public. He wrote first for his own flock, churchmen who had been urged to back the society against his known wishes.

He stresses that his quarrel is not with spreading the Bible itself. His point is that churchmen have their own society for the work, one that gives the Established Church more safety and strength. The tract asks members to stay steady in their duty and to beware calls that would draw them off.
52590-the-night-club:
The Night Club is a comic novel by Herbert Jenkins, the creator of Bindle, published in London in 1918 in a first edition of twenty thousand copies.

The idea of the club begins with Bindle himself, the cockney furniture remover who loves a story above all things. A group of friends had fallen into the habit of drifting to Dick Little's Chelsea flat on Sunday evenings for a smoke, a drink, and a yarn. Among them are Jocelyn Dare, a writer who hates publishers, and Jack Carruthers, who tolerates everyone except Lloyd George. Chapters promise the coming of Sallie, a prime minister who decides to advertise, the Barabbas Club, and a visit to Bindle's own home. A Zeppelin night with the Moggridges and Sallie at the wheel close the fun.
53717-through-the-sikh-war-a-tale-of-the:
Henty marches boys through war in Through the Sikh War, a tale of the conquest of the Punjaub, printed in London by Blackie. Eight plates by Hal Hurst and a map of the Punjaub dress the book. Henty had writ With Clive in India and The Dash for Khartoum. A cover plate shows Percy threatening to shoot the ferrymen.

His preface frames the wars. Province by province the Empire of India was won, he says, and few wars were more brilliant or hard fought than those that ended in the taking of the Punjaub. The Sikhs were a brave and free race, he grants. Their own turbulent soldiery crossed into states under British guard, sure they could master Delhi. It was luck for Britain the fight came before the Mutiny, he holds.
55435-captain-chub:
Captain Chub is a boys' tale by Ralph Henry Barbour, printed in 1909. The Century Company held the rights from 1908 and put it out that September. Relyea drew the pictures, the boys entertaining Mr Ewing among them. Barbour had writ The Crimson Sweater and Harry's Island before this. Twenty-seven chapters run from the stolen run to gifts and farewells.

Letters and plans, then an invitation to Miss Emery, open the tale. Leasing a house-boat and a trip of inspection set the cruise afoot. The Jolly Roger begins her cruise up the Hudson River early. Driven to cover, prisoners, and a new acquaintance crowd the middle. Mr Ewing is outwitted, then the tables turn on the boys. Keeping store, a midnight alarm, and a burglary raise the late stakes. A gipsy camp, clues, and Chub's own adventure close the cruise.
56834-the-polly-page-yacht-club:
The Polly Page Yacht Club is a girls sea tale by Izola Forrester, out in nineteen ten. A Jacobs house of Philadelphia brought the book out that fall. Ruth Brooks hunts for Polly at a launch feast in the first part. Sad strains of two songs tell the guests it is time to go home. Polly brown head shows not in the crowd as Ruth scans the hall.

Parts run through crew pick, fit out, and board of the Hippocampus craft. Three days at sea, Lost Isle, and an anchor drop fill the mid parts. Smuggler Isle, a girl in the sea, and a pearl feast crowd late parts. A race day and the first heat lead to the youth cup win part. Miss Calvert in black silk stands tall in the first hall scene.
60525-the-dinner-club:
The Dinner Club is a book of short stories by Sapper, the pen name of McNeile. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London, Toronto, and New York. McNeile was by then famous as the author of Bull-Dog Drummond. A list of his earlier war and adventure books stands at the front.

The contents are arranged as tales told by members of a club. A barrister's story turns on the decision of a judge in chambers. A doctor's story is headed, in grim joke, a sentence of death. The ordinary man tells of the pipes of death in his turn. A soldier's tale hangs on a bit of orange peel, and a writer's on a house. The Quilt opens the sequence before the professions take their turns.
60838-the-rod-and-gun-club:
The Rod and Gun Club, by Harry Castlemon, closes the Rod and Gun series. The Winston company issued the book at Philadelphia, Chicago, and Toronto. Copyright dates to 1883, under Porter and Coates. A front plate shows the battle with the strikers.

The tale opens with some disgusted boys and a talk in a library. Brigham tells his son Lester that he has provided for the boy's next four years. Lester's idea comes next, then flight and pursuit, and Don's encounter with a tramp. A test of courage and the fight as reported build toward a darker turn. One chapter puts the boys in the hands of the mob. Plans, deserters afloat, and a clue found by Don lead on to the club itself. Casting the fly and a conclusion round out eighteen chapters of adventure.
61888-chinook-the-cinnamon-cub:
Chinook the Cinnamon Cub is a children's nature story by Allen Chaffee, issued in 1924 with pictures by Peter Da Ru. Chaffee had written other animal books, named on the title page, about a snow baby and two young bears. The contents promise twenty chapters of woodland adventure. It opens with a boy and a bear.

Early chapters teach the cubs to swim, under their mother's sharp command in a front picture. A California lion, a home in a squirrel's nest, and a pair of tree mice follow. The cub is lost in fog, plays the clown, and meets an Indian trapper. A raven's nest, a smuggler, and a great quake fill the later heads. The first page sets the scene at dawn in the Oregon woods.
62151-adele-doring-of-the-sunnyside-club:
Grace May North wrote Adele Doring of the Sunnyside Club, published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1919. North founded and edited the real Sunnyside Club of California, and dedicated the book to all happy-hearted girls from ten to fifteen. Florence Young illustrated it. The story opens in spring, with seven girls dancing across April meadows on a holiday. Their first act is to form a club.

The contents show a year of club life. The girls keep a secret sanctum, hold a scrubbing party, and give a surprise party and a birthday feast. They build a Mother Goose play-house, endure examinations, and take vacation days on Pine Island. A little bear, a fish supper, and a trip to the city follow. Later chapters grow graver: a visit to the poorhouse, a mystery solved, and a girl named Eva beginning a new life.
63757-breath-of-beelzebub:
Breath of Beelzebub, a science fiction story by Larry Sternig, first appeared in the magazine Planet Stories in the winter of 1946. The story opens with a strange claim. All that could be drawn from the plants of a doomed planetoid was half an ounce of blue liquor. That was enough to drive a universe mad.

The tale is told by Fleming Ames, who works at a desk handling figures for his employer. A Martian servant brings in a shabby visitor named Slane O'Graeme, who has come to see Mr. Ames and is plainly not welcome. Behind the office scene sits the dangerous drink, which is not, as the visitor explains, a drink exactly. The story plays its pulp premise straight, mixing future office routine, Martians on Earth, and a substance from a planetoid that no longer exists.
69854-the-christmas-makers-club:
The Christmas Makers' Club is a children's Christmas story by Edith Sawyer, published at Boston in 1908. Ada Williamson drew the pictures. A motto verse counts glad things, ending with Christmas bells a-ringing. The book is dedicated to four girls. Its first chapter gathers the club for work and play.

The children make their plans in the frontispiece scene. Chapters follow Prince Gray Owl, what the woods gave, and a round of visiting. A little old lady's doll and the boy in the club vary the tale. Gray Owl plays Santa Claus at the end. The club makes its gifts by hand, and the story teaches the making as much as the giving.
69935-the-safety-first-club:
W T Nichols wrote this boys' novel, published by Penn in 1916 with pictures by F A Anderson. Sam Parker slams out onto the porch on a gray Saturday, in a temper with the weather and everything else.

He had overslept, lost a shoe under the bureau, and found the eggs hard and the oatmeal cold. The contents follow Sam and his club through thirty chapters: the club gets a new name, Poke and Step put their heads together, and Lon discusses crooked thinking. Later come a blizzard, Peter Groche's grudge, and Sam's choice. Nichols built the club on the safety first idea then sweeping factories and railroads. Boys get adventure with a motto inside it.
72584-bulletin-of-the-nuttall-ornitholog:
Bulletin of the Nuttall Ornithological Club, volume seven, is a quarterly journal of bird study printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1882. Allen edited it, with Baird and Coues as his associates. The Nuttall Club was America's first society for the study of birds. Its bulletin carried records and descriptions from observers across the country.

The first number opens with Ridgway on an apparently new heron from Florida. A list of birds seen near Houston, Texas, follows, and a paper on a small bone at the front of the bird's wrist. Brewster writes on the habits and plumage changes of the Acadian owl and its breeding in Massachusetts. New races of Texas birds are described and named. Such pages built American ornithology note by note. This volume preserves a year of that work, when bird study was passing from collectors to science.
72855-the-unpleasantness-at-the-bellona-:
The Unpleasantness at the Bellona Club, a Lord Peter Wimsey mystery by Dorothy Sayers, was copyrighted in 1928. The first chapter is called Old Mossy Face, in club slang. Captain Fentiman flings aside his newspaper and demands what Wimsey is doing in this morgue. Wimsey answers, amiably, that he would not call it that.

Funeral parlour at the very least, he retorts, admiring the marble and palms. Look at the corpses, says Fentiman, and at old Ormsby snoring like a hippopotamus. He quotes a Punch joke about a lord dead two days in his chair. A dead general in an armchair is in fact the case here. Sayers mixes club comedy with a hard question of the hour of death.
75342-tour-of-the-zero-club:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote Tour of the Zero Club, or Adventures Amid Ice and Snow, dated nineteen hundred and two. Street and Smith issued the boys' tale at New York and London. The tale opens on a toboggan slide.

Harry Webb gives his long toboggan, the Buster, a final shove and hops on behind three companions. They race down Doublehead Hill, shouting to hold on. Chapters bring races, a stolen iceboat, and the start of the tour. Jack is lost in the snow, wolves chase the party, and a heavy storm besieges the camp. A fight with reptiles sits oddly among the ice. A black bear and a country dance close the outing.
all-aboard-or-life-on-the-lake-a-sequel-: Oliver Optic continues his Boat Club stories with All Aboard, or Life on the Lake, sending his boys back to boating, camping, and lake adventure. The sequel keeps the club's spirit of pluck, fair play, and practical seamanship, with new scrapes and lessons along the shore. It is a typical Optic boys' book, wholesome, brisk, and full of outdoor incident.
britannica-1911-beefsteak-club:
Beefsteak Club is the subject of a club article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was borne by several clubs formed in London in the seventeen and eighteen hundreds. The first seems to date from 1709, with an actor as its steward. Its members were the chief wits and great men of the nation. Its badge was a gridiron, the tool for grilling steak.

The article gives most space to a later club founded in 1735. A theatre manager at Covent Garden started it after a lord praised his grilled steak. Its members called themselves the Steaks and included Hogarth, Garrick, and Wilkes. The prince of Wales joined in 1785. The club met at theatres and coffee houses as fires forced moves. It ceased to exist in 1867. A modern London club of the name dates from 1876.
britannica-1911-beelzebub:
Beelzebub, a god of the Philistine city of Ekron, is studied in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The Old Testament names him once, in the second book of Kings. King Ahaziah, sick after a fall, sent to ask if he would recover. The name joins Baal, a common word for a god, with Zebub. Scholars have long debated what that second part means.

The article weighs the main guesses about the name. Zebub may be a place name, though no such place is known. More often it is read as the Hebrew word for flies. On that view Baalzebub is the lord of the flies. Flies, as children of summer, were tied to the warmth of the sun. The article cites fly gods in Greek cult as well. A link to the dung beetle of Egypt is also raised.
britannica-1911-caub: Caub, or Kaub, is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau, covered in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Rhine, twenty-eight miles north-west of Wiesbaden, with 2,200 people. The entry notes its two churches, a statue of Bluecher, and a trade based on district wines. Above the town stands the ruin of Gutenfels castle. Facing it, on a rock mid-river, sits the small castle Pfalz, in truth a toll station for Rhine traffic.
britannica-1911-club:
Club has three senses, a thick stick used as a weapon, one of the four suits of playing cards, and an association of persons, and the entry is devoted to the third. By club is meant here an association within the state of persons not united by any natural ties of kinship. Such clubs are found in all ancient states of which detailed knowledge exists. They seem to have dated in one form or another from a very early period.

The rigid system of kin groups, family, gens and phratria, may itself have suggested groups of a more elastic and expansive nature. Clubs were thus an expedient for delivering society from a too rigid principle of crystallisation. A law of Solon, quoted in Justinian's Digest, guaranteed the administrative independence of Greek associations. Greek and Roman clubs are treated first in the article's plan, and modern clubs below.
britannica-1911-green-ribbon-club:
The Green Ribbon Club was one of the earliest of the loose political associations that met in London taverns in the 17th century. The 1911 Britannica entry places it at the King's Head tavern at Chancery Lane End, so it was first called the King's Head Club. It seems to have been founded about 1675.

Its members, the party hostile to the court, wore a bow of green ribbon in their hats as a badge, handy for knowing one another in street brawls. About 1679 the club took its ribbon name. The entry calls its frequenters the extreme faction of the country party: supporters of Titus Oates, touched by the Rye House Plot and Monmouth's rebellion. Roger North is quoted on its open door for proselytes, and Dryden on its drinking. The court, through Thomas Dangerfield, held a list of its members.
britannica-1911-shrub:
Shrub, a word with two unlike senses, is set out in a word study entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. As a plant term it names a bushy plant with a woody stem. Its branches spread thick from the ground and it stays too low to count as a tree. The line between shrubs, trees, and woody herbs is hard to draw.

Holly, yew, and laurel can grow into trees if left to a single stem. Rhododendron and lilac stay true shrubs by nature. The plant word is the same as scrub, for low stunted growth. It shows up in English place names such as Shrewsbury. As a drink term, shrub names a cordial now rare outside country districts. One kind mixes currant juice, sugar, and rum. The drink word comes from an Arabic term for a beverage, kin to sherbet and syrup.
britannica-1911-starodub:
Starodub is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Russia. It lies in the government of Chernigov. The city of Chernigov stands far to the south west. The town is regularly built with broad, straight streets. Large gardens surround the houses on every side. Its people number 12,451 in the count given. They are Little Russians, with about five thousand Jews. Tanning and copper ware making go on in the town.

A trade in corn and hemp runs through Starodub. Those goods go out to Riga and Saint Petersburg. As early as the eleventh century, princes fought over the town. They valued its strong strategic position on the frontier. The Mongols seem to have destroyed it in the thirteenth century. Its name then vanishes from record for a century. Russians and Lithuanians fought over its fortress for years. In the early seventeenth century it became a Polish stronghold.
britannica-1911-uskub:
Uskub, also called Skopia, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the capital of a province in European Turkey. The city stands on the left bank of the river Vardar, at a railway junction. Its population in 1905 was about thirty two thousand. Its people are chiefly Slavs, Turks, and Albanians, with a few others.

The city holds a scenic and key military position at the foot of a valley, the entry says. That valley cuts between two mountain ranges. Main roads run out from it to towns in several directions. Uskub is the headquarters of an army corps and the seat of three bishops of different churches. Its chief buildings include a citadel, the governor's palace, schools, churches, mosques, and a Roman aqueduct. Local trades include dyeing, weaving, and tanning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beelzebub:
Beelzebub, or Baalzebub, was the Philistine god of Accaron, scarcely twenty-five miles west of Jerusalem. King Ochozias tried to consult his oracle in his last illness, and the Old Testament mentions him nowhere else. His name is commonly rendered lord of the flies, whether because he brings flies or, likelier, drives them from sacrifice. Cheyne reads the original as Baal Zebul, lord of the high house, changed in contempt to lord of flies.

In the Gospels the name lingers as Zeboul, and Beelzebub appears as arch-demon and exorcist. Allen argues Mark simply names the demon said to possess Our Lord, while Matthew and Luke fuse clauses to identify Beelzebub with Satan. The fusion seems justified by Mark's next verse, though Allen's reading remains possible. Beelzebub is absent from Jewish literature of the period, where Beliar serves as Satan's alternative name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cisalpine-clu:
English Catholics after 1766 gave up Jacobite hopes and accepted the House of Hanover. Suspicion of Rome's strictness grew, and the Catholic Committee of 1782 to 1792 pressed for emancipation under Lord Petre and Sir John Throckmorton, with Charles Butler as secretary. In 1788 Lord Stanhope drafted a Protestation disclaiming papal deposing power and other ultramontane doctrines. Bishops, priests, and leading laymen signed it.

The Relief Act of 1791 dropped the Protestation oath after bishops condemned it, so a new society formed to keep its principles alive: the Cisalpine Club. Forty to fifty members met four or five times a year over dinner. At first they guarded Catholic interests and helped found a school at Oscott. Soon they became a mere dining club, and after Emancipation in 1829 they re-formed as the Emancipation Club, dissolving seventeen years later.
doe-osti-2583454-high-power-electric-veh:
Technical report from July 2025, by Emin Ucer, Akram Syed Ali, Jason D. Harper, and four colleagues at NREL and Argonne, designs the brain of a high-power EV charging hub. A site energy management system, or SEMS, constantly decides how chargers, solar, batteries, and the grid share power. The eCHIP project built that platform and ran it on two DC hub testbeds of different sizes.

Five core functions structure the design: energy and power management, cost minimization, charge scheduling, grid support, and resilience when the grid drops. Control can be centralized, decentralized, or hybrid, and the report weighs each style against the others. Model predictive control looks ahead rather than reacting. Dashboards and monitoring close the loop for operators. Standards for hubs fill an appendix. As truck and fleet charging scales up, unmanaged hubs would slam local grids; this platform is the coordinating layer meant to prevent that.
doe-osti-2584737-enhanced-h-sub-2-sub-pr:
Maria Gabriela Davila Ordonez wrote LLNL report LLNL-TR-2006805 in July 2025 on making more hydrogen under the ground. The project tests whether organic acids, put into deep rock, can raise the rate at which the rock gives off natural hydrogen gas. Some pages hold protected data made under a U.S. Department of Energy deal, and the report marks those pages clearly.

The team built a test setup and checked that it worked, studied its rock samples, and set a base rate for hydrogen output. It then varied the strength of the acid and watched the effect. Stronger acid action broke down minerals faster and made rock faces more reactive, and hydrogen output rose. The work matters because hydrogen from rocks could be a clean fuel if rates can be raised in a reliable way.
doe-osti-3001510-western-regional-direct:
Chris Moseley of Chevron files a pre-feasibility study, dated 12 November 2025 under cooperative agreement DE-FE0032379, for a Western Regional Direct Air Capture Hub. Direct air capture pulls carbon dioxide straight from the sky; a hub clusters capture plants with shared infrastructure and permanent underground storage. Pre-feasibility is the paper stage: choose technologies, sketch the plant, and test whether the idea deserves real engineering money.

Sections cover the study basis, candidate capture systems, an initial balance-of-plant design concept, safety and security requirements, and the regulations in play. A preliminary life-cycle assessment checks that the hub would remove more carbon than its construction and operation emit, the essential sanity test for any capture project. Data tables size the initial capacity. Storage field work ran in parallel outside the study's funding, with technology descriptions and maturation plans for vendors, 280 Earth among them, collected in appendices.
doe-osti-3013029-prairie-horizon-carbon-:
Energy and Environmental Research Center staff at the University of North Dakota, led by Kevin C. Connors with six co-authors, wrote this final report for the Prairie Horizon Carbon Management Hub, dated January 2026. The report covers December 2023 through November 2025 under cooperative agreement DE-FE0032371. The hub would gather and store carbon dioxide in Stark County, North Dakota, and the study's stated aim was building public confidence in carbon management.

The team screened the county's geology, including storage complexes and a possible carbon dioxide enhanced oil recovery play. They reviewed legacy wellbores, pipeline routes along existing rights-of-way, and the rules around competing pore space claims. A public opinion survey found about 90 percent of respondents aware of carbon capture, with wind power drawing 63 percent support against about 30 percent for solar in the same survey.
doe-osti-3015473-williston-basin-associa:
A University of North Dakota Energy and Environmental Research Center final report documents storing carbon dioxide with associated gas production in the Williston Basin. It ran under agreement DE-FE0031694. It covers February 2019 through September 2025. The field laboratory paired carbon storage with oilfield operations in North Dakota's Bakken region. Steven Smith was principal investigator.

Work packages ran from geology and residual oil zone analysis to an active seismoelectric survey. Fluid behavior studies and life-cycle accounting of capture at gas plants followed. One comparison shows capture at one plant needs 6.07 million standard cubic feet of raw gas. Sales gas comes to 3.94 million standard cubic feet. Emissions come to 0.51 million standard cubic feet of carbon dioxide. Transport and distribution emissions use one factor throughout the analysis. The factor is 7.1 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per thousand standard cubic feet.
doe-osti-3016269-florida-regional-dac-hu:
The University of Illinois Illinois Sustainable Technology Center submitted this final report on February 4, 2026, for award DE-FE0032378. Kevin C OBrien was principal investigator and Jason Dietsch lead engineer. The report covers the feasibility phase of a Florida regional direct air capture hub. Such a hub is a planned cluster of plants that pull carbon dioxide straight from the air.

Sections describe the ownership team, the hub site, transport routes for captured carbon dioxide, and storage sites. Heirloom's capture technology is described as an anchor option. Data tables set out capture potential figures of 60,000 and 1,000,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, and list storage well options for the hub. Conversion offtakers were still at zero in the tables, an honest snapshot of an early-stage plan. Reviewers can judge the site and storage case before design money is spent.
doe-osti-3017565-novel-modular-heat-engi:
Bugra Ertas of GE Aerospace Research led this final report for contract DE-FE0031617, submitted February 9, 2026. The performance period ran from May 2020 to June 2025. The project designed modular heat engines with a supercritical carbon dioxide bottoming cycle, recovering waste heat as extra power. Its turbomachinery was advanced and oil-free, riding on gas bearings instead of lubricated ones.

The report covers the full design chain: test rig, electric machine, permanent magnet rotor, bearing system, rotordynamics, and thermal modeling. Then it is blunt about the ending. All hardware was fabricated and major components procured, but assembly and testing of the rotating system were not achieved, for time and budget reasons. Open risks include proving rotordynamic behavior up to 27,000 revolutions per minute on hybrid gas bearings. Engineers inherit complete drawings and models, plus an honest list of what remains unproven.
doe-osti-3031180-a-play-based-exploratio:
Will Johnson, Daryl-Lynn Roberts, Matt Chester, and Kai Oliver of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign map the human ground for carbon storage in report DOE-UIUC-32366-01, issued April 27, 2026. Nathan D. Webb led the project under agreement DE-FE0032366. Before anyone drills for carbon dioxide storage in the Illinois Basin, planners need a baseline: who lives there, who decides, and what burdens communities already carry.

The study sorts stakeholders from regulators and landowners to advocates and industry. It urges a formal register and charts that sort groups by interest and influence. A regional profile then weighs health and exposure data, such as disability rates, life expectancy, and asthma levels, county by county. Industrial towns often sit closest to landfills, refineries, and freight routes, the report notes.
doe-osti-3031279-a-play-based-exploratio:
Mike Situ, Hannah Veldhuizen, Nathan D. Webb, and colleagues at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign lay out a mapping workflow in report DOE-UIUC-32366-02, issued April 28, 2026. Webb led the work under agreement DE-FE0032366, with Visage Energy. The Illinois State Geological Survey team wanted a repeatable way to find spots where rock, surface, and community conditions all favor carbon dioxide storage. Oil and gas explorers call such a method play-based exploration.

Seven steps carry the workflow: define play elements, gather data, build a geodatabase, set suitability rules, map suitability, draw common risk segment maps, and finish with composite play maps. The test case weighed stacked sandstones, the Mt. Simon and St. Peter, and over 20 play elements, from seal shape and faults to wetlands and karst ground.
doe-osti-3144958-a-play-based-exploratio:
Nathan D. Webb, Hannah J. Veldhuizen, and Carl H. Carman of the Illinois State Geological Survey file the final report for the Illinois Basin play-based exploration project, DOE-UIUC-32366-03, issued April 30, 2026. Webb led the work under agreement DE-FE0032366. The project hunted for the best carbon dioxide storage spots in the basin by stacking maps of rock, surface, and community factors, then grading where they align.

Each play element got a plain definition and a suitability rule. Storage formation thickness counts only rock flagged as a possible reservoir, drawn from well records and geologic models. Confining unit thickness counts the low-flow rock that caps each reservoir. Staff also built a tool with a federal consortium to digitize old well records, and student crews checked the output by hand before it joined the survey database.
doe-osti-3364693-ornl-report-for-hydroly:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4617, by Kellen Springer, Carson Grant, Lindsey Lecrivain, Brian Ticknor, and Jenn Parikh, dates to May 2026. It records laboratory analysis of five hydrolyzed uranium hexafluoride samples, numbered 439451, 438792, 439144, 439616, and 439617. Uranium hexafluoride is enrichment feed gas; reacting it with water converts it to solid compounds the Chemical Sciences Division can measure.

The report documents sample handling and the analytical results for each numbered sample in turn. Such records support nuclear material accounting, since the composition of converted material confirms what a batch of feed contained. The format is a working laboratory record rather than a research paper: identification pages, methods, and measured results for the five samples, kept under the lab's quality practices.
doe-osti-3484643-energy-storage-impacts-:
Pacific Northwest guide PNNL-39529, dated June 2026, helps developers judge energy storage impacts in resilience hubs and other key sites. Adrienne L. S. Rackley, Lin Zeng, and Brittany Y. Davis lead the author team. Resilience hubs keep power for communities during outages.

Metric checks ask whether each measure can be repeated the same way over time. Other checks cover clarity for funders, time fit, and data trust. Sources range from utility records to outage logs. A balanced metric set mixes counted results with judged ones. Hub builders get a fair scorecard for storage value beyond simple cost.
four-boy-hunters-or-the-outing-of-the-gu:
Stratemeyer, writing as Captain Ralph Bonehill, sends four boys on a hunting cruise with their gun club. Chapters promise a sawmill fire, a vanished boat, a wildcat, a cave in the mountain, and a night surrounded by wolves. Rival campers and a forest fire close the outing.

In the cave episode Shep and Snap sit on flat rocks, wet to the knees, weighing their escape. Climbing the shaft they fell down might bring dirt and rocks onto their heads. Snap reasons that the cave's water must reach the surface somewhere. Edward Stratemeyer wrote the tale as a complete story in itself for his boy readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DubeLouisJDepos: A deposition given by Louis J. Dube was taken in Civil Action 82-1686 before the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. A deposition is sworn testimony recorded outside the courtroom, usually in a lawyer's office with a reporter present. The surviving record gives the witness, the case number, and the court, but not the subject of the suit or the date the testimony was taken.
the-high-school-boys-canoe-club:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys' Canoe Club, subtitled Dick & Co.'s Rivals on Lake Pleasant. The contents list chapters such as The Splendid War Canoe, Buying Fuel for a Bonfire, Birch Bark Merchants, Meeting the Fate of Greenhorns, and Trentville, the Awesome. Chapter one opens with Colonel W. P. Grundy lamenting a grand plan in a voice broken with feeling.

Grundy calls the wreck before him one of the grandest enterprises ever conceived by the human mind. Small boys grin and say nothing. He adds that such defeats often come to those who try to educate the masses and raise popular intelligence to a higher level, wiping away a real or imagined tear.
the-parenticide-club:
Ambrose Bierce wrote the four grim tales of The Parenticide Club. The contents list My Favorite Murder, Oil of Dog, An Imperfect Conflagration, and The Hypnotist. My Favorite Murder opens with a narrator who murdered his mother under circumstances of singular atrocity and stood trial for seven years. The judge calls it one of the most ghastly crimes he has had to explain away.

The prisoner's lawyer argues that the earlier murder of an uncle was far worse, and that the later crime shows tender forbearance by comparison. Bierce writes with a straight face and a lawyer's logic. His club of killers treats murder as a fine art and a family duty.
the-s-w-f-club:
Caroline E. Jacobs published The S. W. F. Club in 1912 with the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Cleveland and George W. Jacobs and Company. Its ten chapters run from Pauline's Flag through beginnings, snap-shots and a stay at the manor to the end of summer.

Chapter one finds Pauline hemming a napkin and staring soberly into a rain-swept garden while her sister Patience holds a clearing-up scrape in the garret, singing that a good time is coming. Pauline doubts good times are coming her way, since they always pass by on the main road. She resolves instead to help them on, and the chapter moves toward Uncle Paul's answer and the club's beginnings.
the-sorcery-club: Elliott O'Donnell, known for books on ghosts and haunted houses, published this novel in London with William Rider and Son in 1912. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. Eleven chapters move from How They First Heard of Atlantis through The Black Art of Atlantis, The Tests, and The Initiation. Later titles bring San Francisco ladies, dreams, and Leon Hamar's call on the Martins. The narrative itself does not appear.
